TTS Fine-Tuning: Building a Marathi Storytelling Voice

Our first text-to-speech fine-tuning project — concepts, architecture, pipeline & results

What is Text-to-Speech?

TTS converts written text into spoken audio.

"एक आटपाट नगर होतं"   →   [ TTS Model ]   →   🔊 spoken Marathi

We are not building a TTS model from scratch — that needs thousands of hours of speech and crores in compute. We take a model that already speaks Marathi and fine-tune it to adopt our narrator's voice and storytelling style.

Our goal: a single, consistent female Marathi storyteller voice ("Sunita"), narrating children's stories, trained on ~20 minutes of clean single-speaker audio. A proof-of-concept before any large data investment.

Why This Matters — Applications

A self-hosted, branded narration voice unlocks unlimited audio at zero per-use API cost:

📚 Kids' story apps

Narrate an endless library of Marathi stories in one warm, familiar voice.

🎧 Audiobooks

Convert any Marathi text to audio at scale, overnight, for free.

♿ Accessibility

Screen-reading for low-literacy / visually-impaired users in their own language.

📣 IVR & announcements

Dynamic phone menus, alerts, and notifications without re-recording.

🎓 E-learning

Auto-voiced lessons and quizzes in regional languages.

🏷️ Brand voice

A signature voice used across millions of impressions — owned, not rented.

The same GPU skills and pipeline extend later to LLM story-writing and image/video generation — this project is the first rung.

How a TTS Model Learns Speech

Text does not become sound in one jump. The classic pipeline is three stages:

The conceptual TTS chain. Modern neural models fuse these stages, but the roles still apply.

  • Phonemizer — text → phonemes (sound units). Handles Anusvara (ं), Halant (्), numbers ("५" → "पाच").
  • Acoustic model — learns pitch, pace, rhythm, where to pause (commas matter!).
  • Vocoder / codec — turns the acoustic representation into the final waveform you hear.
The model learns everything it hears. Background hum, echo or clicks get baked into the voice — which is why a clean, single-speaker dataset is non-negotiable.

How a Model Knows It Is "Right" — the Loss

A loss function is a single number measuring how wrong the model's output is. Training = repeatedly nudging weights to make that number smaller. Different architectures use different losses:

Approach A — the GAN / mel-loss family (StyleTTS, VITS, HiFi-GAN)

A Generator produces sound; a Discriminator judges if it is real or fake. The mel-loss compares mel-spectrograms (pitch-aware pictures of audio) of generated vs. real speech.

Mel-loss: measures the difference between generated and ground-truth speech by comparing Mel-spectrograms — visual representations of audio that mimic human pitch perception. This is how StyleTTS/VITS learn — but our model, Parler-TTS, does NOT use it.

Approach B — the token / cross-entropy family (Parler-TTS)

Parler treats audio as a sequence of discrete tokens and predicts them one by one, exactly like an LLM predicts the next word. Its loss is cross-entropy: "how surprised was the model by the correct next audio token?" Lower = better prediction. No mel-loss, no discriminator.

The StyleTTS Approach (Oversimplified)

In StyleTTS, the voice comes from a reference audio snippet, encoded into a "style vector" that conditions generation.

Reference snippet → style encoder → "style vector". Combined with input text in a Transformer–Diffusion–GAN, the output is trained to sound like the snippet.

  • Voice driven by a reference clip, not a text description.
  • Uses diffusion + GAN → mel/adversarial losses. World-class naturalness…
  • …but English only. No native Marathi → wrong tool for our task.

Indic Parler-TTS — Architecture

Parler is an autoregressive language model for audio. Two text inputs go in; a stream of audio tokens comes out and is decoded to a waveform.

Caption → frozen Flan-T5 encoder sets the voice & style. Transcript → tokenizer sets the words. The Decoder LM (the only trained part during fine-tuning) predicts DAC audio tokens; the DAC codec turns them into the waveform.

  • No diffusion, no GAN, no reference clip. Voice is set by a plain-English caption.
  • An autoregressive LM — predicts audio as a token sequence, like Llama predicts words.
  • Trained with cross-entropy over audio tokens — not mel-loss.
  • Fine-tuning mostly updates the Decoder LM; Flan-T5 stays frozen.

Mental model: Parler-TTS is to audio what an LLM is to text — a transformer predicting the next token, where each token is a chunk of sound.

Two Engines, Side by Side

DimensionStyleTTS2 (GAN family)Indic Parler-TTS (token family)
Core mechanismDiffusion + GANAutoregressive audio tokens
Voice controlReference audio clipPlain-English text caption
Training lossMel + adversarial (GAN)Cross-entropy
Marathi support❌ English-only✅ Native (122+ hrs)
AnalogyImage style-transferNext-token LLM, but for sound
Why this distinction matters for the results: because Parler uses cross-entropy, our training graphs show eval/loss and codebook_loss — never mel-loss or discriminator loss. Watching for those would be watching the wrong architecture.

Fine-Tuning vs Cloning

Cloning (training-free)

Give a 5–30s clip, the model mimics it on the fly. Instant, but inconsistent and quality-capped by the base model. Great for a quick demo.

Fine-tuning (updates weights)

Train on a dataset → the voice & style are baked in permanently. Stable, consistent, higher quality — but needs a training run on a GPU.

For a branded voice used millions of times, fine-tuning wins — and that's what this PoC validates. (In the audio section you'll hear both: IndicF5 is a clone; fine-tuned Parler is a real fine-tune.)

Why a GPU is Required

Audio is enormous. At 24,000 samples per second:

24,000 × 60   = 1,440,000     (one minute)
1,440,000 × 5 = 7,200,000     (five minutes)

A 5-minute story = 7.2 million data points. In training you must also hold the gradient (same size) + Adam optimizer states (momentum + variance per parameter) → roughly 3–4× memory, all at once. That's why even a 24 GB GPU can't process a full clip in one pass — and why we segment audio into 2–20 second chunks.

HardwareParallel coresTime for this PoC
Laptop CPU~8–163–7 days (may never finish)
GPU (RTX A5000, 24 GB)~8,000+~1–2 hours
GPUs do thousands of multiply-adds in parallel — exactly the math a neural network is. CPUs do a few at a time. For matrix-heavy training that's the difference between hours and days.

Dataset Format

Parler expects a 3-column dataset. The caption is identical on every row so the model locks onto one voice.

ColumnContentExample
audiomono clip at model sample-rate, 2–20 sec(audio waveform)
textexact Marathi transcript (Devanagari)एक आटपाट नगर होतं.
descriptionEnglish caption — same every rowSunita narrates in an expressive, warm storytelling tone. Very clear audio with no background noise.
  • Single female narrator → one fixed caption across all rows.
  • Caption must contain the phrase "very clear audio" → triggers high-fidelity generation.
  • Clips 2–20 sec (4–12 s sweet spot), clean, no background music.
  • Transcript must match audio exactly — mismatches are the #1 cause of a bad fine-tune.

The Pipeline We Ran — Step by Step

All slow-but-cheap prep runs free on a laptop; we rent the GPU only for the training minutes.

Why split it? RTX A5000 (24 GB) at ~$0.27/hr → the whole job is under ₹45. Data prep needs no GPU, so we never pay for idle GPU time.

Key Training Settings

SettingValueWhy
Base modelai4bharat/indic-parler-tts (0.9B)Native Marathi, Apache 2.0
Epochs5~20 min overfits fast — let eval/loss decide
Steps174Small dataset → few steps per epoch
Precisionbf16A5000 is Ampere → native BF16, avoids NaN
Sample rateread from model.configNever hardcode — resample to model's rate
Text encoderFlan-T5 (frozen)Only the decoder LM learns the voice
LoggingWeights & BiasesLive loss curves + audio samples each eval

How to Read the Output Losses

Four numbers tell the story. Know which direction is "good":

MetricWhat it measuresGood direction
train/lossCross-entropy on training audio tokens — how well it fits what it has seen↓ lower
eval/lossSame, on held-out audio — the real "is it learning?" signal↓ lower
codebook losses (×9)Parler predicts audio across 9 parallel token streams; each must improve↓ lower
WER (word error rate)Generated speech re-transcribed by ASR — % of words wrong↓ lower
CLAPHow well the audio matches its text description↑ higher

The two patterns to recognise

Undertraining: train & eval both still dropping → give it more data/steps. Overfitting: eval rises while train keeps falling → stop. Our run is firmly in the left pattern.

Trust your ears over the number. Each eval step logs generated audio to W&B — pronunciation, voice consistency and artefacts are the final check, not the loss digit alone.

What's working ✅

Falling eval loss + falling codebook losses = the fine-tuning pipeline works. (Illustrative reconstruction of the W&B curves.)

What needs caution ⚠️

WER above 100% looks alarming but is expected here. With only ~20 min of data and 5 epochs, the model has started learning the voice but is heavily undertrained. Train-loss (3.55) sitting below eval-loss (4.27) confirms undertraining, not overfitting — which more data and steps will fix. WER is also notoriously unreliable on tiny TTS fine-tunes.

Conclusion

  • ✅ Pipeline validated — data prep, upload, fine-tune, checkpoint export, all end-to-end in ~4 min for ~₹45.
  • ✅ The model is learning — eval loss and all 9 codebook losses dropping steadily.
  • ⚠️ Not yet a usable voice — WER ~100% means output not yet fully intelligible. Undertrained on 20 min of data.
  • Next lever is data, not tricks — biggest gain comes from more clean audio of the same narrator (45–60+ min) and more steps.

A successful proof of pipeline: it proves the method works end-to-end for ₹45, before any major data or hardware investment. It is not yet a production voice — and that's exactly what a PoC should tell us.

Where This Goes Next

  1. Scale data — 45–60+ min of the same narrator, studio-recorded and owned.
  2. Train longer — more epochs/steps to converge to intelligible speech; watch eval/loss for the overfitting turn.
  3. Re-evaluate — listen to samples + re-check WER / CLAP after each run.
  4. Add voices — male / child narrators, each a selectable caption.
  5. Deploy — host on our server → unlimited stories at zero API cost.
  6. Bigger picture — same GPU + skills extend to LLM story-writing and image/video generation.

Bottom line: the ₹45 PoC de-risked the approach. We now know the pipeline works and exactly what to invest in next — more clean data of one narrator.
